newsitem.title: USA: Cree Research says developes blue laser.
newsitem.headline: Cree Research says developes blue laser.

text.p: Cree Research Inc said Monday it demonstrated an electrically pulsed gallium nitride based blue laser at room temperature which may be used to increase the storage capacity of optical storage systems, such as high-end mass storage optical recording systems.
A commercially viable blue laser could also eventually be used in consumer products such as CD-ROM, CD audio and DVD by increasing storage capacity four or five times.
The shorter wavelength of blue light as compared with longer wavelength red or infrared lasers used today is responsible for the increased storage capability.

The company said the breakthrough was accomplished by scientists who designed and fabricated a device using Cree's silicon carbide wafers combined with a proprietary gallium nitride thin film process.
John Edmond, Cree's co-founder and the senior scientist in charge of the development program, said, "We are elated about demonstrating electrically pulsed laser operation at room temperature."
He added, "This is a milestone toward achieving a commercially viable laser, but we still have a lot of development work ahead of us."
Cree has been working for the past two years to develop its laser device with partial funding from the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA).

DARPA program director, Anis Husain said, "This demonstration is a critical step to realizing a key military component. Short wavelength blue lasers are critical for high data storage military systems and chemical biological reagent sensing, as well as covert communications."
Cree, based in North Carolina, developes silicon carbide based semiconductors which have potential advantages in certain optoelectronic, RF, microwave, power and high temperature applications.
A DVD is a Digital Versatile Device, which is expected to be the next generation of laser disc.
